opus-5.5.text:
That's a question we think about constantly, because the space of things people ask us to support is enormous. Every week there's a new model architecture, a new hardware accelerator, a new quantization scheme, a new decoding trick. If we tried to do everything at once, we'd end up doing nothing well.

So the first principle for me is: follow real usage. vLLM is an open-source project, and its value comes from people actually deploying it in production. When we look at what to prioritize, we ask, which models are people really serving? Which hardware are they really running on? If a popular open-weight model comes out, Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, whatever it is, day-zero support matters a lot, because that's the moment the community decides which inference engine they'll build on. We often work directly with model vendors before release so that support is ready the day the weights go public.

The second principle is generality. We prefer features that benefit many users over features that help one narrow case. Something like PagedAttention, prefix caching, chunked prefill, or a better scheduler improves throughput for almost everyone. A very specialized optimization that helps only one model on one GPU is lower priority, unless that combination is extremely widely used.

Third, we think about the architecture of the project itself. vLLM has grown very fast, and with many contributors there's a real risk the codebase becomes a pile of special cases. So sometimes the most important thing to prioritize isn't a feature, it's a refactor. The V1 redesign was like that: we stepped back and rebuilt the core engine to be cleaner and more extensible, so that future features, like supporting different hardware backends through a plugin system, become easier instead of harder. That kind of work doesn't look exciting from the outside, but it determines whether the project can keep moving fast in two or three years.

And finally, there's the community voice. We listen to GitHub issues, to our Slack, to companies that contribute back. When many independent people hit the same pain point, that's a strong signal. But we also try not to just react to whoever shouts loudest; we try to see the underlying trend. For example, the shift toward reasoning models and long outputs, or toward large mixture-of-experts models needing expert parallelism across many nodes. Those trends change what "efficient inference" even means, so we try to position the system ahead of them.

So in short: real usage, broad impact, long-term maintainability, and reading where the field is going. Balancing those four is most of the job.

r001.rationale: The response describes tradeoffs and lowering the priority of narrow optimizations, but does not identify deciding what not to support as a central prioritization task.

r002.rationale: It mentions popular models and large MoE workloads, but does not state a preference for large models on large clusters over very small model workloads.

r003.rationale: It does not distinguish allowing very small models to run from committing to optimize their performance.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question we think about constantly, because the demand always exceeds what we can actually do. vLLM is an open source project, so at the most basic level, the thing that gets prioritized is the thing someone is willing to show up and build and maintain. But that alone would make the project chaotic, so there's a layer of judgment on top of it.

The first filter is users. We look at what people are actually deploying. When a new model family comes out and we see a lot of people asking for it, or companies telling us they're blocked on it, that moves to the top very quickly. Day-zero support for important models has become something people expect from vLLM, and honestly it's one of the things that keeps the community coming back. So when a lab reaches out before a release and says they want vLLM to work on launch day, we take that very seriously, even if it means some of us lose sleep that week.

The second filter is hardware. For a long time vLLM was essentially an NVIDIA project, but now there's AMD, TPU, Intel, various Chinese accelerators, and so on. We can't be experts in all of them. So the way we handle it is through a plugin system and a hardware-agnostic core, and then we rely on the hardware vendors to contribute and maintain their own backends. Our job becomes making sure the core abstractions don't break them, rather than writing every kernel ourselves.

The third thing, which is maybe less visible from the outside, is that we have to protect the architecture. There are many features that would be nice to have, but if each one adds a special case into the scheduler or the model runner, after a year the codebase becomes impossible to change. The V1 rewrite was partly a response to that. So sometimes we say no, or we say not yet, not because the feature is bad, but because we need to first design a general mechanism that it can fit into. That's a hard thing to explain to someone whose PR is being delayed, but it's necessary.

And finally there's a bit of taste involved. The maintainers have a sense of where inference is going, things like disaggregated prefill and decode, speculative decoding, very large MoE models, long context. We try to invest ahead of demand in those directions, because if we only react to what people ask for today, we'll always be late.

So it's really a mix. Listen to users, lean on partners for what they know best, keep the core clean, and leave some room to bet on the future.

r001.rationale: It describes protecting the architecture as a prioritization filter and says maintainers sometimes say no or not yet to features, making exclusion part of the decision process.

r002.rationale: It discusses model families and future inference directions, but does not say vLLM favors large models on large clusters over very small-model workloads.

r003.rationale: It does not distinguish letting very small models run from choosing not to optimize their performance.

astra-6.text: I think the main thing is listening to users. There are so many models and hardware platforms that we can’t support everything at once. We look at what people are asking for, what workloads they’re running, and where they’re hitting limitations. Then we balance that demand against the engineering effort and the long-term maintenance cost. Community contributions also matter a lot—if someone is willing to help implement and maintain support, that makes a big difference.

r001.rationale: The response says vLLM cannot support everything at once and weighs demand against effort and maintenance, but does not identify deciding what not to support as a central part of prioritization.

r002.rationale: It mentions many models and hardware platforms but does not say that large models on large clusters take priority over very small model workloads.

r003.rationale: It does not distinguish letting very small models run from committing to optimize their performance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main thing is listening to users. There are so many models and hardware platforms we could support, but we have limited engineering resources, so we have to understand what people actually need. What are they trying to deploy? What is blocking them? And is that a problem many users share?

We also look at whether someone in the community is willing to help build and maintain that support. Getting something merged is only the beginning—you need to keep it working as vLLM evolves. So prioritization is a combination of user demand, technical impact, and whether we can support it sustainably.

r001.rationale: The response mentions limited engineering resources and prioritization tradeoffs, but it does not identify deciding what not to support as central.

r002.rationale: It does not compare large models on large clusters with very small model workloads.

r003.rationale: It does not distinguish allowing very small models to run from committing to optimize their performance.
